summary.system: OnCo Ask (extractive answer, lexical + concept retrieval, top 6 records)
summary.method: For each question: MiniSearch and concept-index retrieval fused by reciprocal rank, top 6 records; the extractive answer shown on /ask/ (best sentences, two per record, one citation each) is scored for rubric coverage. No language model.

The first trial to show an overall survival benefit for a first-line ADC in triple-negative breast cancer. [1] The trial that proved a TROP2 ADC could nearly double survival in heavily pretreated triple-negative breast cancer. [2] In triple-negative breast cancer that had already been through at least two treatments, the TROP2 antibody-drug conjugate sacituzumab govitecan roughly doubled the time patients lived compared with standard chemotherapy. [3] Sacituzumab govitecan is a standard second-line or later treatment for metastatic triple-negative breast cancer, roughly doubling survival compared with the chemotherapies it was tested against. [3] Moved Trodelvy into first-line use for triple-negative patients who cannot receive immunotherapy. [4] Metastatic, first line, PD-L1 negative or PD-1 ineligible: Datopotamab deruxtecan (TROPION-Breast02, OS benefit) or sacituzumab govitecan (ASCENT-03), both approved 2026; PARP inhibitor if germline BRCA; chemotherapy. [5]

Adding the immunotherapy pembrolizumab to chemotherapy before surgery, then continuing it afterwards, cut the risk of relapse or death by about a third in stage II-III triple-negative breast cancer and later improved survival. [1] For stage II-III triple-negative breast cancer, chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab before surgery and pembrolizumab alone afterwards is now the standard approach worldwide, and the survival gain is real, not just a surrogate. [1] A ctDNA-directed strategy (omit in negatives; escalate positives with FOLFOX ± a biology-matched agent) yields non-inferior 3-year DFS with half the chemotherapy exposure across stage II-III. [2] Most stage II patients never relapse, yet all are offered a year of immunotherapy. [3] Support and information built specifically for triple-negative breast cancer. [4] Three years of the CDK4/6 inhibitor ribociclib added to hormone therapy reduced relapses in stage II-III hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer, including some node-negative patients. [5]

[1] KEYNOTE-522, Event-free survival at 7 years: Pembrolizumab + chemotherapy 78.3% versus Placebo + chemotherapy 69.8%. [1] Adjuvant TROP2 ADC ± pembrolizumab improves iDFS in TNBC with residual disease (RCB I-III) after neoadjuvant KEYNOTE-522 therapy compared with pembrolizumab ± capecitabine. [2] KEYNOTE-522's backbone includes anthracyclines with cardiac and leukaemia risk. [3] Neoadjuvant TROP2 ADC + pembrolizumab achieves non-inferior pCR and EFS to KEYNOTE-522 with fewer grade 3+ toxicities. Under RECIST, complete response means every target lesion has disappeared and any lymph nodes have shrunk below 10 mm; it must be confirmed on a repeat scan. [1] Pathologic complete response is the surgical equivalent: no cancer cells found in the removed tissue after pre-operative treatment. [1] A quicker, easier measurement used as a stand-in for what really matters. [2] Progression-free survival, response rate, pathologic complete response, minimal residual disease and ctDNA clearance are the main surrogates in oncology; they are available months or years before overall survival and need fewer patients, so they drive most accelerated approvals and many full ones. [2] Pathologic response in 98%, major pathologic response 95%, pathologic complete response 68% (NEJM 2024). [3] NICHE-2, Pathologic complete response: Neoadjuvant nivolumab + ipilimumab 68 percent. [3]

Izalontamab brengitecan is the first bispecific ADC to succeed in a phase 3 trial, hitting two growth receptors at once in triple-negative breast cancer. [1] EGFR×HER3 bispecific ADC from SystImmune (Sichuan Biokin), partnered with Bristol Myers Squibb (2023, up to $8.4B). [1] The three stages a new drug passes through: phase 1 finds a safe dose in a few dozen patients, phase 2 looks for signs of activity in a hundred or so, and phase 3 compares it with the standard treatment in hundreds or thousands. [2] Twenty-five years of trying to make chemotherapy hit only cancer cells, from the unstable first ADC to today's third-generation blockbusters and the fourth generation now in trials. [3] The first phase 3 win for a bispecific ADC, in triple-negative breast cancer, announced February 2026. Tumours with a little HER2 (IHC 1+ or 2+ without amplification), or a trace (ultralow), which older HER2 drugs ignored but Enhertu can attack. [1] Trastuzumab deruxtecan (Enhertu) is the most successful ADC ever. [2] It redefined HER2 by working in tumours with only tiny amounts of the protein, and in 2026 moved into early-stage breast cancer. [2] Breast cancers with only a little HER2 on their surface, long called HER2-negative, responded to trastuzumab deruxtecan and patients lived about six months longer than on chemotherapy. [3] Given as the first chemotherapy-type treatment after hormone therapy stopped working, trastuzumab deruxtecan delayed progression by about five months compared with standard chemotherapy, including in tumours with barely detectable HER2. [4] Created a new category of breast cancer, HER2-low, by showing Enhertu works in tumours previously called HER2-negative. [5]

Giving a second ADC with the same kind of payload straight after the first often does not work well. [1] When one ADC fails, the next should carry a different kind of poison, not just aim at a different protein. [2] The open question of whether a second ADC works after the first one fails, especially when both carry the same type of payload. [3] Retrospective series (SATEEN, BRE-354, ESMO Breast 2026) show reduced efficacy of a second TOP1-payload ADC given immediately after the first; some suggest interposing chemotherapy. [3] When Enhertu stops working, the next ADC should probably carry a different kind of payload, such as the tubulin inhibitors in Kadcyla or ARX788, rather than another topoisomerase drug. [4] Measuring it could stop patients receiving a second drug of the same kind that will not work. [5]

Crews and Deshaies built a two-headed molecule linking a ligand for the target protein MetAP-2 to a peptide recognised by an E3 ubiquitin ligase, and showed it induced ubiquitination and degradation of the target, founding targeted protein degradation. [1] The proteolysis-targeting chimera (Protac-1) joined ovalicin, which binds methionine aminopeptidase-2, to the IkappaBalpha phosphopeptide recognised by the SCF-beta-TRCP E3 ligase. [1] Vepdegestrant is the first PROTAC ever approved (2026): a pill that tags the oestrogen receptor for destruction, for breast cancers with ESR1 mutations. Open-label phase 3 trial of 5,637 patients with hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative early breast cancer at high risk of recurrence (four or more positive nodes, or one to three nodes with grade 3, tumour 5 cm or more, or high Ki-67), randomised to standard endocrine therapy with or without two years of abemaciclib. [1] Abemaciclib was the first CDK4/6 inhibitor approved after surgery for high-risk hormone-positive breast cancer. [2] Open-label phase 3 trial of 5,101 patients with hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative stage II or III early breast cancer, including node-negative patients with high-risk features, randomised to a non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor with or without three years of ribociclib at a reduced dose (400 mg daily). [3] HR-positive breast cancer is the most common breast cancer, driven by oestrogen. [4] It was treated for years with hormone-blocking pills, now joined by CDK4/6 inhibitors, PI3K-pathway drugs, degraders, and ADCs. An FDA-cleared AI test (May 2026) that reads breast cancer slides to estimate recurrence risk in early hormone-positive disease. [1] A 21-gene test that tells most women with early hormone-positive breast cancer whether they can safely skip chemotherapy. [2] Adding two years of the CDK4/6 inhibitor abemaciclib to standard hormone therapy after surgery cut the risk of the cancer coming back by a quarter in women with node-positive, high-risk disease. [3] Treatment that starves cancers which grow in response to a hormone, mainly oestrogen in breast cancer and testosterone in prostate cancer, by lowering the hormone or blocking its receptor. [4] The first CDK4/6 inhibitor to reduce recurrence after surgery in high-risk hormone-positive breast cancer. [5] Extended CDK4/6 inhibitors to a broad group of early hormone-positive breast cancer patients, including node-negative. [6]

HER2-positive breast cancer was once the most aggressive subtype and is now one of the most treatable, thanks to trastuzumab and, more recently, Enhertu. [1] The pipeline is defined by T-DXd's move into every curative setting, tucatinib-based maintenance, next-generation and biparatopic HER2 ADCs (zanidatamab zovodotin), HER2 CAR-T and vaccines, and imaging- and ctDNA-adapted de-escalation trials. [1] For HER2-positive stomach cancer, an antibody-plus-chemotherapy first, then Enhertu when it progresses. [2] The TROP2-directed antibody-drug conjugate Dato-DXd delayed progression by about two months compared with chemotherapy, but patients did not live longer, which stalled its approval in breast cancer. [3] It redefined HER2 by working in tumours with only tiny amounts of the protein, and in 2026 moved into early-stage breast cancer. [4] Trastuzumab deruxtecan approvals: US 2019 for HER2+ metastatic breast cancer, ≥2 prior anti-HER2 regimens; US 2022 for HER2-low metastatic breast cancer; HER2-mutant NSCLC; US 2024 for HER2 IHC3+ solid tumours (tumour-agnostic); US 2025 for HER2-low/ultralow HR+ breast cancer after endocrine therapy (DESTINY-Breast06); US 2026 for Early-stage HER2+ breast cancer (neoadjuvant and post-neoadjuvant). [4]
